units.title: Forecourt guy: update
units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: Update on the man who stands at the edge of my forecourt light every night. Tonight I went out with a bag of rubbish as an excuse. He's a local guy, maybe sixty, waiting for his son to pick him up after the late shift at the fish plant. He stands there because it's where the son pulls in. He said good evening. I said good evening. Mystery solved, very embarrassing for me.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: taro this is the most wholesome thing that has happened on this forum all month and I am including the time someone's dog learned to open a fridge. also I'm coming in for noodles at three, chapter deadline tomorrow, please have the spicy ones

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Good result. Logged as: subject identified, nil further. That's how most of mine end too, and nobody posts those. For the record I'm glad you went out with the bin bag rather than calling it in. Saves a lot of paperwork.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Thank you for posting the resolution, taro. This matters more than it seems: stories that end in 'it was a man waiting for a lift' rarely get written up, so the ones that don't end that way look more common than they are. I'm going to quote you in the merged thread, if that's all right.

units.title: Edge of the light (merged thread)
units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: I've merged the six 'someone standing at the edge of the light' threads into this one, so the front page is about night shifts again. Taro's update is linked from here. Please post your own experiences here rather than starting new threads. Lamp Hours is company on the night shift, not campfire stories, so keep it kind and keep it real. Drink some water.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Since this is the merged thread, my long post. Part 1. Peripheral vision is poor at colour and detail but very good at motion and shape, and fatigue makes it worse at telling them apart. The edge of a pool of light is exactly where your eyes are switching between day and night vision. That transition zone produces false figures. It's not a theory; it's how rods and cones work.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Part 2. The cluster itself is a reporting effect. Before the first post, nobody had a phrase for it. Once 'standing at the edge of the light' existed, people had a box to put their 3am glimpses in. Reports rise. That doesn't mean anyone is lying; it means language shapes noticing. Taro's man waiting for a lift would have been in this thread a week ago. n of 1, but a telling one.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Noted, Dmitra, and I don't disagree about eyes. For the record mine isn't peripheral. It's on a fixed camera, recorded, at the edge of the floodlit area by bay 14. I patrolled. Nil found. That's three times on the old camera and once on the new one. I'm not saying what it is. I'm saying it's on a recording, not in my eye.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: That's fair, and it's the one I can't explain from here. A camera has its own version of the transition zone: auto-exposure, compression, low light noise clumping into shapes at the edge of a bright area. But I'd need to see the footage. If your company will let you, I'd genuinely like to.

units.author: hollow_signal
units.text: Merge them all you like... it doesn't change what's happening... every one of these is at a lit place with dark around it... a forecourt, a dock, a car park... and now an island... I've said before I can't go into detail. But you can all see the shape of it by now, can't you...

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Every story on a night-shift forum is set at a lit place with dark around it, Hollow. That's what night shifts are. We're the people in the lit places. You might as well say every fish story happens near water. Source, please, for anything you've actually seen yourself.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Adding mine for completeness since it's merged now. Not a figure, a van. Same van that idled four hours at the edge of our car park lights at the start of the month turned up on the verge at the Brackwater junction this morning on my drive home. Engine on, cab dark. Not standing at the edge of the light so much as parking at it. Probably someone sleeping rough.

units.author: lh_miner_vellmark
units.text: End of shift, on the bus. Underground, the edge of the light is the edge of your cap lamp, a metre and a half. Old hands step inside it, never out. Tradition. When your lamp moves your edge moves, so there's never anyone standing at it. Only on the surface does the edge stay still. Make of that what you like. Bus is here.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Not a person, just my dogs. The back corridor at the kennel has one bulb at the near end and nothing beyond the fire door, and the dogs stop exactly where the light stops. I've tested it: moved the lamp a metre further and they went a metre further. So whatever it is, for them it's the dark, not the place. Which is nicer, honestly.

units.author: hollow_signal
units.text: Orla wants a source... fine... I know someone who knows the people who bought the island in the Sound. They're preparing for when it comes out of the dark for good. That's why they need it cleared. That's why the lights. They know where it stops. They're coming. They're already standing at the edge of every...

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: I've removed HollowSignal's post above for unsourced claims about real-world people and for scaremongering, which is the second time. Hollow, you're welcome to talk about your own nights. You're not welcome to frighten people who are alone at work. I'm locking this thread and starting a fresh one with the same rules. Water, everyone.

units.title: Edge of the light (merged thread, continued)
units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: continuing the merged thread here, with the same rules. Your own experiences only, no claims about what anyone else is planning, and please read Dmitra's two posts in the old thread first. If you just want to talk about your shift, there's a flask thread on the front page that is much nicer.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Thanks, Ines. Small observation from the radio side: this week on the overnight show we've had five callers describe 'someone at the edge of the light'. Three of them used that exact phrase, which as far as I know started on this forum. That's not proof of anything except that people read Lamp Hours, which is lovely, and also a bit of a problem.

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text: ok I'll put mine in even though I'm still half sure it was a runner. Tonight at the hospital rank, end of the lit bit by the bins, someone standing, like they're waiting for a cab but not coming to the cab. I flashed my lights. Nothing. Pulled forward. Nobody. Nurse I know got in the back and said I looked like I'd seen a parking ticket anyway

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Orla, that's the clearest example of what I meant yesterday. The phrase travels faster than the experience. I'd add, gently, that this is also a forum where most of us are awake at hours the body isn't designed for. If anything, it's remarkable there aren't more reports. Go to bed after shift, everyone. Properly. Curtains.

units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: I've been reading an old keeper's logbook from a light in the Sound, transcribed online. Every few nights, in the remarks column, the same few words: 'walkers on the shore road, did not answer.' He never reports it to his Board. He just writes it down and trims the lamp. I find I understand him. From my gallery the beam ends, and the land beyond it is simply land, and sometimes there's a walker. Did not answer.

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Beautifully put, and I'll allow it because it's literature, not a scare. But a gentle reminder to all: walkers on a shore road at night are almost always walkers on a shore road at night. The keeper's era had no streetlights and plenty of people walking home from the pub.

units.author: dc_5_lorna
units.text: just an update from me love since I mentioned the bus at the depot that kept its lights on with nobody aboard, the engineers say it's a timer on the interior lights that's gone funny, same thing as the relay at my flats, so there you are, it's always a timer, I'm off to bed, the frost on the depot yard this morning was like icing sugar

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Dmitra, I'm sure you're right about people. The dogs haven't read Lamp Hours, though, and they've stopped at the back corridor since before the phrase existed. I'm not saying that proves anything. I'm saying I'd like an explanation that covers the beagles too.

units.title: What's in the flask tonight?
units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Morale thread, because the front page has gone gloomy. Port Ammet General, B corridor, 01:15. In my flask: tomato soup from a tin, with a slice of buttered bread folded into the top like a lid, which my nan swore by. In the vending machine on B: one packet of salt and vinegar, guarding the empty spiral like a lighthouse. What's in yours?

units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: Flask? Darling, I'm standing next to an oven. Tonight it's cardamom buns proving under a cloth and a mug of milky coffee going cold on the flour bin because I keep forgetting it. The whole harbour smells of sugar and diesel. I would send you a bun if the postal service were faster than proving.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: Sweet tea, too sweet, made by one of our residents who still gets up to make it for 'the night girl' at half three every night, and I would never tell her I don't take sugar. She sits with me in the kitchen while I drink it and tells me about her husband's motorbike. It's the best part of the shift. Sorry, long post.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Peppermint tea, because the ward is too warm and my feet hurt and peppermint is the only thing that feels like a window. Half a cereal bar I found in my pocket from last week. The intercom has been blessedly silent since they replaced the button. Back to it.

units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: energy drink number two and a protein bar that tastes like sweetened plasterboard, because my target tonight is 210 an hour and the scanner says I'm on 196 and it's judging me. break's ten minutes. I spent four of them reading this. worth it. back in aisle 41

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: this is the best thread on the front page and I'm pinning it. In my own flask: chamomile, which I recommend to every customer and then ignore myself by having a double espresso at four. Pharmacist, heal thyself. Carry on, all of you.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Not a flask, a teapot, because I'm at home and have no excuse. Lapsang, which smells like a bonfire in a library. I'm reading a book I've read four times, in which a man stays up all night by a fire waiting for news, and it's much more comforting than it sounds. Hello, all of you working people.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: call centre flask report: decaf, because my supervisor read an article. also between calls: a caller just asked me to hold while she found her account number and I listened to her kettle boil, then her toaster, then she came back and said 'sorry, breakfast'. ma'am it is half past eleven at night here. respect.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Black coffee from a truck stop on the county line that's been on the hotplate since about the invention of the wheel. Two of their honey rolls on the seat beside me. Advice from an old hand: in a cold snap, keep your flask inside your coat, not in the cab door, or it'll be iced coffee by mile 80. Ten-four, good buddies.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Update from B corridor: someone has bought the salt and vinegar. The spiral is empty. The lighthouse has gone out. I'm taking it personally. On the bright side, A&E sent me a doughnut for moving a wardrobe-sized patient who fell over on the ice. Good night all. Mind the frost.

units.title: New boarder, same corridor
units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: New boarder tonight: Pickle, a three-year-old beagle who has never been here before and knows nothing about our back corridor. At 02:15 I walked her to the yard the long way, down the back. She sat at the same spot the others do, by the last bulb, and would not get up. I carried her. She's 14 kilos of offended beagle. The vet tech thinks there's a smell from the drains.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Jo, I've known a lot of dogs on the road, and a beagle that won't follow its nose somewhere is a beagle that's smelled something it doesn't like. Drains is a good bet. Skunk under the building is a better one out your way this time of year. Stopping by your town Thursday, I'll bring a torch.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: I want to say something helpful but mostly I want a photo of 14 kilos of offended beagle. between calls: our office dog won't go in the server room, and that turned out to be because of the high-pitched whine from the air conditioning. maybe something electrical down that corridor? dogs hear stuff we can't

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Hana's suggestion is a good one. Dogs hear well up into the ultrasonic, and failing ballasts, transformers and some pest deterrents whine up there. A cheap bat detector would show it. If there's a tone that starts at the last bulb, that's your answer. If there isn't, at least you've ruled it out.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Borrowed a bat detector from the science teacher across the road. Walked the corridor with it at 01:30. Nothing above the hum of the freezer in the food room, which the dogs walk past fine. Drains guy comes Monday. Pickle went home today. Her owner said she 'never sits for anything'. Well.

units.title: 4,000 words in 20 hours, a live diary
units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: Situation report: chapter three due 09:00 tomorrow. Words remaining: 4,000. Energy drinks remaining: 3. The lab motion lights are behaving, the centrifuge is not. I will be updating this thread so that when I fail, there is a historical record. Please send encouragement and, if possible, a functioning brain.

units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: Spicy noodles set aside behind the counter. Also a banana, which you didn't ask for. You need a banana. I'm not your mother but I am the person who sells you four energy drinks a night. Go write.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: From a sleep technician: the last 1,000 words written after 04:00 will need rewriting anyway. Sleep two hours at 03:00, set two alarms, and you'll write the last section better and faster. I know you won't. I'm saying it so it's on the record when you tell us later I was right.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: Submitted. 08:52! Chapter three is in. It is 11,212 words long and at least 9,000 of them are good. I slept two hours at three like dmitra said (you were right, I hate it) and the last section came out in ninety minutes. The centrifuge is still broken. I don't care. I'm going to sleep for a week. Thank you all, genuinely.

units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: Congratulations. Banana worked. I've put a celebratory egg custard aside for you, it's the last one, a man in a hi-vis tried to buy it and I told him it was reserved for a doctor of philosophy. He seemed impressed.

units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: Congratulations, love! In the bakery we say a dough that's been knocked back and left alone always comes up better, and I think that's true of students too. I'm making a batch of honey twists tonight in your honour. Nobody here will know why. That's the best kind of celebration.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: I'm framing 'you were right, I hate it'. Well done, Rin. Now please, genuinely, keep normal hours for a few days. Your circadian rhythm is currently somewhere over the ocean. Curtains, no screens, and if the motion lights do anything strange this week, it's because you're tired.

units.title: A quiet one
units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: Just a short one. The lady I've written about, the one who said 'that's for me' when the door intercom buzzed, died tonight in her sleep. Very peacefully, about one o'clock, with her daughter holding her hand and the radio on low. I sat with them both for a while. She made me tea last night, too sweet. I wanted you all to know. Sorry, back to work.

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Liv, thank you for telling us. What a good way to go, with her daughter and the radio, and you there. Look after yourself tonight. Have a glass of water, eat something, and if you need to talk at the end of your shift, we're all here.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: I'm so sorry, Liv. It sounds as though she was looked after properly right to the end, which isn't true for everyone and should be. Grief on a night shift is a strange, lonely thing; please let someone drive you home if you can.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: From the morgue run lad: the people who do your job are the ones who make mine bearable. A cup of too-sweet tea is a lovely last thing to share. Sorry for your loss, Liv. Someone at my place always opens a window for a minute, after. Old habit. Might help.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Sending you a hug from the ward, Liv. We open the window too, same as the porter's lot. Nobody ever told me why. I think it's just to let the night in for a moment and remind yourself it's still going on out there. Back to it, but thinking of you.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Only just seen this, Liv. I'm sorry. When one of our old boarders goes, we keep their name on the whiteboard for a week. Silly, maybe. But it helps the night staff. Maybe write hers down somewhere you'll see it. Hugs from the kennel.

units.title: Frost on the harbour, butter in the cold room
units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: It's gone properly cold here at last. The harbour is steaming in the floodlights like a pan of soup, the boats are furred white, and the butter in the cold room is so hard I'm laminating with a rolling pin and my whole body weight. The van driver who used to sleep outside now comes in for a roll and sits by the oven.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Confirmed from gate 7: the harbour is steaming. Visibility in the yard down to about 80 m by 04:00. Patrolled, nil found, very cold. Rolls received at 04:10, still warm, much appreciated. The camera on bay 14 has frost on the housing, so I've no picture at all on that one tonight.

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: I walked past your window at the end of my shift and saw the van driver by your oven, asleep with a roll in his hand. I didn't wake him. Off-duty housekeeping: this is the Coriveth I like. I'll be in for my loaf at six as usual.

units.title: Live: 300 miles of nothing, anyone up?
units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Anybody up? I've got 300 miles of the flats ahead of me and the radio's all static and preachers. Cold snap's made the road ring under the tyres. Next lit stop is the grain town at mile 212. Talk to me about anything. Coffee, dogs, the price of diesel. Ten-four.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: I'm up, Merle. Three dogs asleep, one awake and judging me, a spaniel called Mo who thinks he's in charge. You're about forty miles from me if you're past the junction. Did you get the honey rolls from the county line place? Keep talking, I'm doing the laundry.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: here, merle, between calls. it's my last hour and nobody's ringing so I'm all yours. what do long-haul people think about in 300 miles of nothing? genuine question, I think about what I'd do with a lottery win and then I get to about item four and run out

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Hana, mostly you think about the next stop. Then about your back. Then about every dog you ever had. Jo, got the rolls, ate both by mile 30, no regrets. Road's empty. Not a car in either direction for an hour. Moon's down. Just the lines coming at you in the headlights, one after another, like counting sheep that don't let you sleep.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: That's the prettiest thing anyone's said about road markings. Mo says hello. When you get to the grain town, the diner by the elevator does a pie you'll want, and they keep the lot lit all night, the full width. Sensible people. You could pull in for an hour.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Might do that. Radio's saying ice on the overpass outside the grain town, so I'm slowing right down. Hands are cold even with the heater going. Back in a bit, need both of them on the wheel. Keep the thread warm for me.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: jo, is it just me or has merle been on 'typing...' for about twenty minutes? the little pencil's been next to his name through three of my calls. I keep refreshing like an idiot. it must be a very long thought about pie. merle if you're dictating with frozen hands, just send it, we'll forgive the typos

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Not just you. It's still there. There's a dead stretch past the elevators where nothing gets a signal, maybe forty miles. Phones do that, freeze on the last thing they were doing. He's done this before, he'll pop up from the diner with a photo of pie. Mo's asleep now, finally.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: pencil's gone. nothing posted. probably hit the dead stretch like you said and the app gave up. I'm off shift, sun's coming up here. night merle, wherever you've pulled in, eat the pie, post the photo. jo, thanks for the company. sleep well

units.title: Anyone else work somewhere they can't see the ground at night?
units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: Light chat for the front page. I run a tower crane on night lifts, 60 m up. From the cab the city's all lit roads and windows, but directly under me, the site is black: floodlights point at the load, not the ground. I can't see where my own feet would land. I've got used to it. Anyone else? Crane cabs, roofs, gantries, ships, top bunks?

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Not me personally, I'm on the ground with a torch, but our gantry crane drivers say exactly the same. They work off the spreader lights and the radio. One of them told me the first week up there he kept looking down and seeing nothing and it made him feel like the crane was floating. Then he stopped looking down.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Opposite problem. I can see nothing but ground. Four acres of lit tarmac and the odd trolley. What I can't see is anything above about three metres, because the floodlights blind you upward. Control says that's why the pigeons always win.

units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: Ha, pigeons. We get gulls on the jib at night, sleeping on the counterweight like it's a cliff. They don't mind the floods at all. Dock guard, your gantry man has it right: you stop looking down. Look at the load, the hook, the signaller's lamp. The ground's somebody else's job.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: Our home is on a hill and the night office is on the top floor. When the frost is like this, the town below is all orange dots and then nothing beyond the last street, just the mine's headgear lit up on the ridge. I don't mind not seeing the ground. It makes the building feel like a boat. Nice thread, thank you.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: The hospital's on a hill above Port Ammet and from the top corridor window you can see the whole harbour, the ferry lights tied up for the night, and the Carrow Point light sweeping round every ten seconds, way out. Can't see the hospital car park though, it's round the back, which is where I actually need to be. Priorities.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Ninth floor, respiratory. The windows don't open and they're tinted, so at night they're basically mirrors: I see myself and the ward and a faint city behind. Some patients find that frightening, waking up and seeing a room in the window. I turn the lamp down and the city comes back. Back to it.

units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: top of the racking on the cherry picker, level 6, about 11 m. the aisle lights are on motion sensors so if nobody's below you, the floor goes dark and you're just in your little cage of light with a pallet of washing powder. it's oddly peaceful till the scanner beeps. great thread

units.author: lh_miner_vellmark
units.text: I work under the ground, so I can't see the ground either, technically. Or the sky. Seven hundred metres of rock overhead and a cap lamp. You get used to it. When I come up at the end of shift I always look at the sky for a minute before I get on the bus. Liv says I do the same at home.

units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: Seven hundred metres down beats sixty up, Anders, I concede. Love these. Porter, I'd swap my view for a lighthouse sweeping past the corridor window any night. From the cab the city is just lit boxes, windows and roads and yards, and the dark is the bit in between. You end up watching the boxes.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Not a worker, just an insomniac in a flat above my own bookshop. The street is lit, but the shop below is dark, and at three in the morning I listen to it the way you'd listen to a sleeping house: the boiler, the shelves settling, a book sliding over. I can't see a thing down there. I know every sound. That's a kind of seeing.

units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: From the gallery, the beam goes out over the sea and the rocks directly beneath the tower are the darkest place for a mile. Light is generous to things far away and miserly to things close. I've worked here eleven years and I still couldn't tell you what the foot of my own tower looks like at night. I've stopped wondering.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: office is on the fourth floor of a business park and the car park lights go off at midnight to save money, so after that the window's just black with my own face in it and a headset. I've started keeping the blind down. not because of anything. I just don't like doing my eyeliner-free face at myself for seven hours

units.title: The intercom did it once more
units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Small thing. The ward intercom, quiet since they replaced the call button, spoke once tonight at 03:05. One name, clearly. Not the old patient's name; a different one, nobody on our ward, nobody I know. Then nothing. Maintenance are on in the morning. I'm noting it here because I said it had stopped, and I'd rather be honest. Back to it.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Thank you for being honest about it. Hospital intercoms usually share a backbone with other wards and the main switchboard; a crossed line or a ward on another floor paging someone would come out as a single clear name. The fact that it was a different name makes me more confident it's a crossed page, not less.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: Ours has been quiet since the electrician found the damp junction box. Not a peep, even tonight. I'm glad you posted, though; I always liked that you and I had matching intercoms. I hope maintenance find something simple. Maybe it's catching.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Our pagers did the same last winter, broadcasting a name from another hospital entirely because some genius had programmed the wrong group. Two porters spent a night looking for a Dr Hennessey we have never employed. Ten to one it's the switchboard.

units.title: The night the yard went dark
units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: This time last night the power went at work. Yard floods first, then aisles. Emergency lights only came on in half the building. They told us to drop scanners and walk to the dock doors, so 60 of us stood in the bays in the lorry headlights for forty minutes while it was minus four. Nobody talked much. The Post wrote it up today and mostly got it right.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Saw your lot from our side of the shared yard. Our car park lights went at the same time. I've never seen so many people stand so still. Couple of your drivers kept their cab lights on for you, which was decent. Control made me do a foot patrol of a pitch black car park in the meantime, which was less decent.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Forty minutes standing in the cold in the middle of a night shift is genuinely hard on the body. Make sure your managers know people should have been given somewhere warm. And that 'nobody talked much' is a normal response: we go quiet in sudden dark. It's old wiring, not a sign of anything.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: A&E had three of your lot's cousins in today, figuratively speaking: one tripped over a pallet in the dark at another depot, two slipped on ice going to their cars. All fine, all wrapped. Glad your managers sent you to the doors rather than letting you pick in the dark. Wear your hi-vis on the ice.

units.author: dc_5_lorna
units.text: oh love I heard about that on the night bus home, the driver said half your shift were stood out on the dock in the cold, I hope they gave you all a hot drink after, you'd think with all those lorries they'd have a heater somewhere, mind how you go on the ice

units.title: A caller on the overnight show
units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Something from last night's overnight show on Sound FM, which I listen to most nights. A caller, a man, quite calm, began talking about the island in the Sound where they're clearing the trees. He said a first name, as if he knew one of the workers, and was about to say more when the line went quiet and Orla played a record. I've thought about it all day. I may well have misheard.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: That was me, and yes, I cut him. Not because of anything spooky. We don't let callers name private people on air, especially people who can't answer for themselves, and especially not workers on a job that's been in the papers. I'm not repeating the name. I'm still not buying any of the island stuff. I'd just rather not be the one who puts a stranger's name on the radio.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: That's entirely fair and I'm glad you did. I should have guessed it was a matter of policy. I won't speculate about the name, which I'm not sure I heard properly anyway. I only felt, at three in the morning, that it would be a lonely thing to have your name said on the radio while you were somewhere you couldn't hear it.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Good call, Orla. A first name is also the most common coincidence there is. Say any common name on a radio show and someone listening will know a person called that. If anyone does have family on that job, please don't let a half-heard call frighten you; that's the whole point of cutting it.

units.author: hollow_signal
units.text: Interesting that the producer cut it so quickly... almost like she knew what he was going to say... I'm not saying anything. I'm only noticing that the name was cut and the island is still lit...

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: Orla has explained a normal broadcasting rule. Hollow, implying she's hiding something is exactly what got your last post removed; this is your final warning before a suspension. Locking this one now, since the question has been answered and the people it's about deserve some quiet. Thank you, Orla and awake_at_3.
